<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Default" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2" COLOR="#0000FF"><B>THE STOCK MARKET ENJOYED SOLID GAINS</B> </FONT> </P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Default" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2">The U.S. stock market rallied following the presidential election in November to post a second consecutive year of solid returns. The gains in the final two months of 2004 capped a year that began with solid
advances in stock indexes but was marked in the middle months by investors' uncertainty about the sustainability of economic growth. The broad stock market, as measured by the Dow Jones Wilshire 5000
Composite Index, ended the 12 months with a return of 12.6%.</FONT> </P>


<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Page Number Center" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2">Gains came in many sectors of the market. The strongest performers were energy-related stocks, which were buoyed by higher prices and increased demand for oil. Generally, small-capitalization stocks outpaced
large-caps, and value stocks--those with prices considered low relative to company earnings, book value, and other measures--outpaced their growth counterparts.</FONT> </P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Default" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2">International stocks, particularly those in emerging markets, posted outstanding returns compared with U.S. stocks. The strong gains abroad were enhanced for investors in the United States by the weakening
of the U.S. dollar against most other major currencies. (A weaker dollar means that returns in other currencies translate into more dollars for U.S.-based investors.)</FONT> </P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Default" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2" COLOR="#0000FF"><B>YIELDS ROSE FOR SHORT-TERM BONDS, FELL FOR LONG-TERM ISSUES</B> </FONT> </P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Default" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2">At the beginning of 2004, bond investors expected the year to bring higher interest rates across the maturity spectrum. Their expectations were based on increasingly strong economic reports, rising corporate
profits, and a belief that the Federal Reserve Board would soon raise the target for short-term interest rates to keep inflation at bay. The actual
result, however, was quite different at the short and long ends of the maturity range.</FONT> </P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Default" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=2>Yields of longer-maturity bonds closed
the year slightly below their starting points. A series of disappointments in the labor
market, record prices for crude oil, and continuing geopolitical turmoil kept bond market
volatility high. At year-end, the 10-year U.S. Treasury note yielded 4.22%, 3 basis points
(0.03 percentage point) </FONT></P>


<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Page Number Center" FSL="Project" -->
<P ALIGN="Left"><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=1>2 </FONT></P>
<P STYLE="page-break-after:always">
</P>

<!-- MARKER PAGE="sheet: 4; page: 4" -->
<HR SIZE=5 COLOR=GRAY NOSHADE>



<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=2>below its 4.25% yield at the start of
the period. Overall, the taxable investment-grade bond market, as measured by the Lehman
Brothers Aggregate Bond Index, returned 4.3%. Across the maturity spectrum, corporate
bonds, particularly those from below-investment-grade issuers, generally did better than
government securities. The Lehman High Yield Index returned 11.1%. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=2>Yields of shorter-maturity securities,
which are generally more closely tied to the Fed&#146;s interest rate moves, rose
significantly. As anticipated, the Fed began to exercise its monetary policy to avert any
significant surge in inflation. Beginning in June, the Fed raised its target for the
federal funds rate from 1.00%, a historical low, to 2.25% through five separate
quarter-point increases. The yield of the 3-month Treasury bill, a proxy for money market
yields, more than doubled during the 12 months, from 0.92% to 2.21%. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Head Left-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
<P ALIGN=LEFT><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2" COLOR="#0000FF"><B>THE FUND SUCCESSFULLY MET
ITS OBJECTIVE</B> </FONT> </P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=2>As expected, Vanguard 500 Index Fund
closely tracked the performance of its unmanaged target index throughout 2004, ultimately
lagging the index by just 0.2 percentage point. (The gap was 0.1 percentage point for
Admiral Shares.)The fund returned 3.4% in the first six months, as the stock market moved
within a fairly narrow trading range. Early on investors seemed enthusiastic about stocks,
but in March a more cautious atmosphere emerged as concern grew over rising energy prices
and the economy. In the second half of 2004, the fund posted a 7.1% return as the economy
showed mixed signs of strength. Much of this gain came in the fourth quarter, when the
fund rose 9.2% amid a post-election stock market surge. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Default" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=2>All 12 index sectors had positive
returns for the year. The best-performing sectors were &#147;other energy&#148;
(+37.5%)&#151;home to companies involved in exploration, production, transportation, and
marketing of energy-related products&#151;and integrated oils (+28.6%), which includes
global giants such as ExxonMobil, ChevronTexaco, and ConocoPhillips. Despite their
relatively small weightings, these two sectors&#146; hefty gains added considerably to the
index return. Consumer discretionary stocks (+14.1%) and financial services issues
(+10.7%) also contributed prominently to the overall return. Consumer discretionary stocks
benefited from the unwavering strength of consumer spending, and financial services stocks
weathered rising interest rates to perform respectably as a group. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Page Number Center" FSL="Project" -->
<P ALIGN="Right"><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=1> 3</FONT></P>
<P STYLE="page-break-after:always">
</P>

<!-- MARKER PAGE="sheet: 5; page: 5" -->
<HR SIZE=5 COLOR=GRAY NOSHADE>



<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=2>As always, a few sectors
underperformed the broad market. The lagging sectors were: Health care (+1.3%), beset by
concerns over life-threatening pharmaceutical side effects, beginning with the withdrawal
of arthritis drug Vioxx from the marketplace; consumer staples (+8.1%); and technology
(+2.7%). </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Head Left-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
<P ALIGN=LEFT><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2" COLOR="#0000FF"><B>AN ENDURING RECORD OF
INDEX-TRACKING CONSISTENCY</B> </FONT> </P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Default" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=2>Over the long term, the strategy of
tracking an unmanaged index has shown itself to be as powerful as it is simple. As you can
see in the table below, over the past ten years your fund has produced an average return
of 12.0% a year, 2.2 percentage points more than the average result for its large-cap core
peers&#151;most of which are actively managed. This performance advantage translates into
a difference of more than $5,500 in the ending value of a hypothetical $10,000 initital
investment. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=2>The fund&#146;s ability to capture
almost all of the target market&#146;s return is a credit to the skills of the advisor,
Vanguard&#146;s Quantitative Equity Group, as well as to low operating or transaction
costs. The dedicated experts in the Quantitative Equity Group have developed proprietary
portfolio construction and trading methodologies that have kept the fund&#146;s return
very close to that of the index. It&#146;s an impressive feat, because the index is not
burdened by real-world operating or transaction costs. Although the fund does incur these
expenses, its ten-year annualized return is just one-tenth of a percentage point less than
that of the S&amp;P 500 Index. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Default" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=2>Although the stock market has now
enjoyed two consecutive years of gains after a brutal two-year bear market for stocks,
nobody knows when the tough times may return again, or how long they&#146;ll last. As I
have counseled on a number of occasions in my reports to you, the best way to weather
these storms and achieve long-term investment success is to stick with a carefully chosen
portfolio of stocks, bonds, and short-term reserves appropriate for your situation.
Avoiding the temptations of the latest &#147;fad&#148; or &#147;hot&#148; investments is
also prudent. </FONT></P>

<TR VALIGN=TOP>
<TD WIDTH="1%" ALIGN="LEFT" BGCOLOR="#CCEEFF"><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=2>&nbsp;</FONT></TD>
<TD WIDTH="99%" ALIGN="Left" BGCOLOR="#CCEEFF" VALIGN="Middle"><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=2>&nbsp;</FONT></TD></tr>

<TR VALIGN=TOP>
<TD WIDTH="1%" ALIGN="LEFT" BGCOLOR="#CCEEFF"><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=2>&nbsp;</FONT></TD>
<TD WIDTH="99%" ALIGN="Left" BGCOLOR="#CCEEFF" VALIGN="Middle"><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=2><B>GLOSSARY OF INVESTMENT
TERMS <br>&nbsp;</B></FONT></TD></tr>
</table>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para (List) Flush Lv 0- Arial" FSL="Default" -->
     <P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2" COLOR="#0000FF"><B>Beta.</B> </FONT><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2"><B>
</B>A measure of the magnitude of a fund&#146;s past share-price fluctuations in
relation to the ups and downs of a given market index. The index is assigned a
beta of 1.00. Compared with a given index, a fund with a beta of 1.20 typically
would have seen its share price rise or fall by 12% when the index rose or fell
by 10%. A fund&#146;s beta should be reviewed in conjunction with its R-squared
(see definition below). The lower the R-squared, the less correlation there is
between the fund and the index, and the less reliable beta is as an indicator of
volatility. </FONT></P>


<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Page Rule Single" FSL="Default" -->
     <HR ALIGN=LEFT WIDTH=100% SIZE=1 NOSHADE>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Default" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2" COLOR="#0000FF"><B>Earnings Growth Rate.</B> </FONT> <FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2">The
average annual rate of growth in earnings over the past five years for the stocks now in a
fund. </FONT> </P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Page Rule Single" FSL="Default" -->
     <HR ALIGN=LEFT WIDTH=100% SIZE=1 NOSHADE>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Default" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2" COLOR="#0000FF"><B>Expense Ratio.</B> </FONT> <FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2">The percentage
of a fund&#146;s average net assets used to pay its annual administrative and advisory
expenses. These expenses directly reduce returns to investors. </FONT> </P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Page Rule Single" FSL="Default" -->
     <HR ALIGN=LEFT WIDTH=100% SIZE=1 NOSHADE>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Default" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2" COLOR="#0000FF"><B>Foreign Holdings.</B> </FONT> <FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2">The
percentage of a fund&#146;s equity assets represented by stocks or depositary receipts of
companies based outside the United States. </FONT> </P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Page Rule Single" FSL="Default" -->
     <HR ALIGN=LEFT WIDTH=100% SIZE=1 NOSHADE>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Default" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2" COLOR="#0000FF"><B>Median Market Cap.</B> </FONT> <FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2">An indicator
of the size of companies in which a fund invests; the midpoint of market capitalization
(market price x shares outstanding) of a fund&#146;s stocks, weighted by the proportion of
the fund&#146;s assets invested in each stock. Stocks representing half of the fund&#146;s
assets have market capitalizations above the median, and the rest are below it. </FONT> </P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Page Rule Single" FSL="Default" -->
     <HR ALIGN=LEFT WIDTH=100% SIZE=1 NOSHADE>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Default" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2" COLOR="#0000FF"><B>Price/Book Ratio.</B> </FONT> <FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2">The share
price of a stock divided by its net worth, or book value, per share. For a fund, the
weighted average price/book ratio of the stocks it holds. </FONT> </P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Page Rule Single" FSL="Default" -->
     <HR ALIGN=LEFT WIDTH=100% SIZE=1 NOSHADE>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Default" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2" COLOR="#0000FF"><B>Price/Earnings Ratio.</B> </FONT> <FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2">The ratio
of a stock&#146;s current price to its per-share earnings over the past year. For a fund,
the weighted average P/E of the stocks it holds. P/E is an indicator of market
expectations about corporate prospects; the higher the P/E, the greater the expectations
for a company&#146;s future growth. </FONT> </P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Page Rule Single" FSL="Default" -->
     <HR ALIGN=LEFT WIDTH=100% SIZE=1 NOSHADE>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para (List) Flush Lv 0- Arial" FSL="Default" -->
     <P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2" COLOR="#0000FF"><B>R-Squared.</B> </FONT><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2"><B>
</B>A measure of how much of a fund&#146;s past returns can be explained by the
returns from the market in general, as measured by a given index. If a
fund&#146;s total returns were precisely synchronized with an index&#146;s
returns, its R-squared would be 1.00. If the fund&#146;s returns bore no
relationship to the index&#146;s returns, its R-squared would be 0. </FONT></P>


<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Page Rule Single" FSL="Default" -->
     <HR ALIGN=LEFT WIDTH=100% SIZE=1 NOSHADE>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Default" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2" COLOR="#0000FF"><B>Return on Equity.</B> </FONT> <FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2">The annual
average rate of return generated by a company during the past five years for each dollar
of shareholder&#146;s equity (net income divided by shareholder&#146;s equity). For a
fund, the weighted average return on equity for the companies whose stocks it holds. </FONT> </P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Page Rule Single" FSL="Default" -->
     <HR ALIGN=LEFT WIDTH=100% SIZE=1 NOSHADE>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Default" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2" COLOR="#0000FF"><B>Short-Term Reserves.</B> </FONT> <FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2">The
percentage of a fund invested in highly liquid, short-term securities that can be readily
converted to cash. </FONT> </P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Page Rule Single" FSL="Default" -->
     <HR ALIGN=LEFT WIDTH=100% SIZE=1 NOSHADE>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Default" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2" COLOR="#0000FF"><B>Turnover Rate.</B> </FONT> <FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2">An indication of
the fund&#146;s trading activity. Funds with high turnover rates incur higher transaction
costs and may be more likely to distribute capital gains (which may be taxable to
investors). </FONT> </P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Page Rule Single" FSL="Default" -->
     <HR ALIGN=LEFT WIDTH=100% SIZE=1 NOSHADE>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para (List) Flush Lv 0- Arial" FSL="Default" -->
     <P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2" COLOR="#0000FF"><B>Yield.</B> </FONT>
<FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2">A snapshot of a fund&#146;s income from interest and dividends. The yield,
expressed as a percentage of the fund&#146;s net asset value, is based on income
earned over the past 30 days and is annualized, or projected forward for the
coming year. The index yield is based on the current annualized rate of income
provided by securities in the index. </FONT></P>


<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Page Rule Single" FSL="Default" -->
     <HR ALIGN=LEFT WIDTH=100% SIZE=1 NOSHADE>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Page Number Center" FSL="Project" -->
<P ALIGN="Right"><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=1>7 </FONT></P>
<P STYLE="page-break-after:always">
</P>

<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=2>This table presents returns for your

distributions <I>and </I>sold all shares at the end of each period. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=2>Calculations are based on the highest
individual federal income tax and capital gains tax rates in effect at the times of the
distributions and the hypothetical sales. State and local taxes were not considered.
After-tax returns reflect the reduced tax rates on ordinary income (including qualified
dividend income) and short-term capital gains that became effective as of January 1, 2003,
and on long-term capital gains realized on or after May 6, 2003. (In the example, returns
after the sale of fund shares may be higher than those assuming no sale. This occurs when
the sale would have produced a capital loss. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=2>The calculation assumes that the
investor received a tax deduction for the loss.) </FONT></P>

Shares only; returns for other shares classes will differ. Please note that your actual
after-tax returns will depend on your tax situation and may differ from those shown. Also
note that if you own the fund in a tax-deferred account, such as an individual retirement
account or a 401(k) plan, this information does not apply to you. Such accounts are not
subject to current taxes. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Default" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=2>We believe it is important for you to understand the impact of costs on your investment. All mutual funds have operating expenses. As a shareholder of the fund, you incur ongoing costs, which include costs
for portfolio management, administrative services, and shareholder reports (like this one), among others. Operating expenses, which are deducted from a fund's gross income, directly reduce the investment
return of the fund.</FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Default" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=2>A fund's expenses are expressed as a percentage of its average net assets. This figure is known as the expense ratio. The following examples are intended to help you understand the ongoing costs (in dollars)
of investing in your fund and to compare these costs with those of other mutual funds. The examples are based on an investment of $1,000 made at the beginning of the period shown and held for the entire
period.</FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Default" -->

<P ALIGN=LEFT><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2" COLOR="#0000FF"><B>STATEMENT OF NET ASSETS</B> </FONT> </P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=2>This Statement provides a detailed
list of the fund&#146;s holdings, including each security&#146;s market value on the last
day of the reporting period. Securities are grouped and subtotaled by asset type (common
stocks, bonds, etc.) and by industry sector. Other assets are added to, and liabilities
are subtracted from, the value of <I>Total Investments </I>to calculate the fund&#146;s
<I>Net Assets</I>. Finally, <I>Net Assets </I>are divided by the outstanding shares of the
fund to arrive at its share price, or <I>Net Asset Value (NAV) Per Share</I>. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=2>At the end of the Statement of Net
Assets, you will find a table displaying the composition of the fund&#146;s net assets.
Because all income and any realized gains must be distributed to shareholders each year,
the bulk of net assets consists of <I>Paid-in Capital </I>(money invested by
shareholders). The amounts shown for <I>Undistributed Net Investment Income </I>and
<I>Accumulated Net Realized Gains </I>usually approximate the sums the fund had available
to distribute to shareholders as income dividends or capital gains as of the statement
date, but may differ because certain investments or transactions may be treated
differently for financial statement and tax purposes. Any <I>Accumulated Net Realized
Losses</I>, and any cumulative excess of distributions over net income or net realized
gains, will appear as negative balances. <I>Unrealized Appreciation (Depreciation) </I>is
the difference between the market value of the fund&#146;s investments and their cost, and
reflects the gains (losses) that would be realized if the fund were to sell all of its
investments at their statement-date values. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Default" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=2>The fund provides a complete list of
its holdings four times in each fiscal year, at the quarter-ends. For the second and
fourth fiscal quarters, the lists appear in the fund&#146;s semiannual and annual reports
to shareholders. For the first and third fiscal quarters, the fund files the lists with
the Securities and Exchange Commission on Form N-Q. Shareholders can look up the
fund&#146;s Forms N-Q on the SEC&#146;s website at www.sec.gov. Forms N-Q may also be
reviewed and copied at the SEC&#146;s Public Reference Room (see the back cover of this
report for further information). </FONT></P>

<H1 ALIGN=LEFT><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2" COLOR="#0000FF"><B>NOTES TO FINANCIAL STATEMENTS</B> </FONT> </H1>


<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=2>Vanguard 500 Index Fund is registered
under the Investment Company Act of 1940 as an open-end investment company, or mutual
fund. The fund offers two classes of shares, Investor Shares and Admiral Shares. Investor
Shares are available to any investor who meets the fund&#146;s minimum purchase
requirements. Admiral Shares are designed for investors who meet certain administrative,
servicing, tenure, and account-size criteria. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para (List) Flush Lv 0- Arial" FSL="Default" -->
     <P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2" COLOR="#0000FF"><B>A.</B> </FONT><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2"><B>&nbsp;
</B>The following significant accounting policies conform to generally accepted
accounting principles for U.S. mutual funds. The fund consistently follows such
policies in preparing its financial statements. </FONT></P>



<TABLE WIDTH=100% CELLPADDING=0 CELLSPACING=0 BORDER=0>
               <TR VALIGN=TOP>
               <TD WIDTH=2%><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2"><B>1.</B> </FONT> </TD>
               <TD WIDTH=98%><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2"><B>Security Valuation: </B>Securities are valued as of the close of trading on the New
              York Stock Exchange (generally 4:00 p.m. Eastern time) on the valuation date.
              Equity securities are valued at the latest quoted sales prices or official closing
              prices taken from the primary market in which each security trades; such
              securities not traded on the valuation date are valued at the mean of the latest
              quoted bid and asked prices. Securities for which market quotations are not
               readily available, or whose values have been materially affected by events
              occurring before the fund's pricing time but after the close of the securities'
              primary markets, are valued by methods deemed by the board of trustees to
              represent fair value. Investments in Vanguard(R)Market Liquidity Fund are valued
              at that fund's net asset value. Temporary cash investments acquired over 60
              days to maturity are valued using the latest bid prices or using valuations based
              on a matrix system (which considers such factors as security prices, yields,
              maturities, and ratings), both as furnished by independent pricing services.
              Other temporary cash investments are valued at amortized cost, which
              approximates market value.</FONT> </TD>
               </TR>
               </TABLE>
               <BR>


<TABLE WIDTH=100% CELLPADDING=0 CELLSPACING=0 BORDER=0>
               <TR VALIGN=TOP>
               <TD WIDTH=2%><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2"><B>2.</B> </FONT> </TD>
               <TD WIDTH=98%><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2"><B>Futures Contracts:</b>The fund uses S&amp;P 500 Index futures contracts to a
               limited extent, with the objectives of maintaining full exposure to the stock
               market, enhancing returns, maintaining liquidity, and minimizing transaction costs. The fund
               may purchase futures contracts to immediately invest incoming cash in the
               market, or sell futures in response to cash outflows, thereby simulating a fully
               invested position in the underlying index while maintaining a cash balance for
               liquidity. The fund may seek to enhance returns by using futures contracts instead of the
               underlying securities when futures are believed to be priced more attractively
               than the underlying securities. The primary risks associated with the use of futures contracts are
               imperfect correlation between changes in market values of stocks held by the
               fund and the prices of futures contracts, and the possibility of an illiquid market.</FONT> </TD>
               </TR>
               </TABLE>
               <BR>


<TABLE WIDTH=100% CELLPADDING=0 CELLSPACING=0 BORDER=0>
               <TR VALIGN=TOP>
               <TD WIDTH=2%><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2"><B>&nbsp;</B> </FONT> </TD>
               <TD WIDTH=98%><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2">Futures contracts are valued at their quoted daily settlement prices. The
              aggregate principal amounts of the contracts are not recorded in the financial
              statements. Fluctuations in the value of the contracts are recorded in the
              Statement of Net Assets as an asset (liability) and in the Statement of Operations
              as unrealized appreciation (depreciation) until the contracts are closed, when
              they are recorded as realized futures gains (losses).</FONT> </TD>
               </TR>
               </TABLE>
               <BR>


<TABLE WIDTH=100% CELLPADDING=0 CELLSPACING=0 BORDER=0>
               <TR VALIGN=TOP>
               <TD WIDTH=2%><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2"><B>3.</B> </FONT> </TD>
               <TD WIDTH=98%><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2"><B>Repurchase Agreements:</b> The fund, along with other members of The
               Vanguard Group, may transfer uninvested cash balances to a pooled cash
               account, which is invested in repurchase agreements secured by U.S.
               government securities. Securities pledged as collateral for repurchase
               agreements are held by a custodian bank until the agreements mature.
               Each agreement requires that the market value of the collateral be sufficient
               to cover payments of interest and principal; however, in the event of default
               or bankruptcy by the other party to the agreement, retention of the collateral may
               be subject to legal proceedings.</FONT> </TD>
               </TR>
               </TABLE>
               <BR>


<TABLE WIDTH=100% CELLPADDING=0 CELLSPACING=0 BORDER=0>
               <TR VALIGN=TOP>
               <TD WIDTH=2%><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2"><B>4.</B> </FONT> </TD>
               <TD WIDTH=98%><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2"><B>Federal Income Taxes: </B> The fund intends to continue to qualify as a regulated
              investment company and distribute all of its taxable income. Accordingly, no
              provision for federal income taxes is required in the financial statements.</FONT> </TD>
               </TR>
               </TABLE>
               <BR>


<TABLE WIDTH=100% CELLPADDING=0 CELLSPACING=0 BORDER=0>
               <TR VALIGN=TOP>
               <TD WIDTH=2%><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2"><B>5.</B> </FONT> </TD>
               <TD WIDTH=98%><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2"><B>Distributions</B>: Distributions to shareholders are recorded on the ex-dividend date.</FONT> </TD>
               </TR>
               </TABLE>
               <BR>

               <TD WIDTH=98%><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2"><B>Security Lending:</B> The fund may lend its securities to qualified institutional
              borrowers to earn additional income. Security loans are required to be secured
              at all times by collateral at least equal to the market value of securities loaned.
              The fund invests cash collateral received in Vanguard Market Liquidity Fund, and
              records a liability for the return of the collateral, during the period the securities
              are on loan. Security lending income represents the income earned on investing
              cash collateral, less expenses associated with the loan.</FONT> </TD>

              is accrued daily. Security transactions are accounted for on the date securities are
              bought or sold. Costs used to determine realized gains (losses) on the sale of
              investment securities are those of the specific securities sold.</FONT> </TD>

              each class separately bears certain class-specific expenses related to maintenance
              of shareholder accounts (included in Management and Administrative expenses)
              and shareholder reporting. Marketing and distribution expenses are allocated to
               each class of shares based on a method approved by the board of trustees.
              Income, other non-class-specific expenses, and realized and unrealized gains and
              losses on investments are allocated to each class of shares based on its relative
              net assets.</FONT> </TD>

     <P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2" COLOR="#0000FF"><B>B.</B> </FONT><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2"><B>&nbsp;
</B>The Vanguard Group furnishes at cost investment advisory, corporate
management, administrative, marketing, and distribution services. The costs of
such services are allocated to the fund under methods approved by the board of
trustees. The fund has committed to provide up to 0.40% of its net assets in
capital contributions to Vanguard. At December 31, 2004, the fund had
contributed capital of $13,931,000 to Vanguard (included in Other Assets),
representing 0.01% of the fund&#146;s net assets and 13.93% of Vanguard&#146;s
capitalization. The fund&#146;s trustees and officers are also directors and
officers of Vanguard. </FONT></P>


<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para (List) Flush Lv 0- Arial" FSL="Project" -->
     <P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2" COLOR="#0000FF"><B>C.</B> </FONT><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2"><B>&nbsp;
</B>Distributions are determined on a tax basis and may differ from net
investment income and realized capital gains for financial reporting purposes.
Differences may be permanent or temporary. Permanent differences are
reclassified among capital accounts in the financial statements to reflect their
tax character. Temporary differences arise when certain items of income,
expense, gain, or loss are recognized in different periods for financial
statement and tax purposes; these differences will reverse at some time in the
future. Differences in classification may also result from the treatment of
short-term gains as ordinary income for tax purposes. </FONT></P>

redemptions&#151;in which shareholders exchange fund shares for securities held by the
fund rather than for cash. Because such gains are not taxable to the fund, and are not

financial position of Vanguard 500 Index Fund (the &#147;Fund&#148;) at December 31, 2004,
the results of its operations for the year then ended, the changes in its net assets for
each of the two years in the period then ended and the financial highlights for each of
the five years in the period then ended, in conformity with accounting principles
generally accepted in the United States of America. These financial statements and
financial highlights (hereafter referred to as &#147;financial statements&#148;) are the
responsibility of the Fund&#146;s management; our responsibility is to express an opinion
on these financial statements based on our audits. We conducted our audits of these
financial statements in accordance with the standards of the Public Company Accounting
Oversight Board (United States). Those standards require that we plan and perform the
audit to obtain reasonable assurance about whether the financial statements are free of
material misstatement. An audit includes examining, on a test basis, evidence supporting
the amounts and disclosures in the financial statements, assessing the accounting
principles used and significant estimates made by management, and evaluating the overall
financial statement presentation. We believe that our audits, which included confirmation
of securities at December 31, 2004 by correspondence with the custodian and broker and by
agreement to the underlying ownership records for Vanguard Market Liquidity Fund, provide

<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=2>The three Vanguard small-cap index
funds tracked their indexes with precision, providing returns within 0.2 percentage point
of their index results. In addition, the returns of the index funds were superior to the
average returns produced by their peer groups. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Default" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=2>Each fund&#146;s total return is based
on the change in net asset value plus any income or capital gains distributions during the
year. The table on page 6 provides details. The table also includes the returns of each
fund&#146;s VIPER shares&#151;exchange-traded shares that were launched on January 26,
2004. Since their inception, the new shares have produced returns similar to those of
their benchmarks. If you hold any of the funds in a taxable account, you may wish to refer
to page 18 for after-tax returns. </FONT></P>

<P STYLE="background-color:aliceblue;"><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2"><B>Admiral&#153; Shares</B><BR>
A lower-cost class of shares available
to many longtime shareholders and to those with significant investments in the fund.<BR><BR>
<B>Institutional Shares</B><BR>
This class of shares carries even
lower expenses and is available for a minimum investment of $10 million.<BR><BR>
<B>VIPER&reg; Shares</B><BR>
Traded on the American Stock Exchange,
VIPERs&reg; are available only through brokers. The table on page 1 shows VIPER returns
based on both the AMEX market price and the net asset value for a share. </FONT> </P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=2>Despite their impressive results, none
of the index funds distributed capital gains during the past 12 months, enhancing their
after-tax returns. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Head Left-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
<P ALIGN=LEFT><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2" COLOR="Blue">STOCK MARKET ENJOYED SOLID
GAINS </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=2>The U.S. stock market rallied
following the presidential election in November to post a second consecutive year of solid
returns. The gains in the final two months of 2004 capped a year that began with solid
advances in stock indexes but was marked in the middle months by investors&#146;
uncertainty about the sustainability of economic growth. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Default" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=2>Gains came in many sectors of the
market. The strongest performers were energy-related stocks, which were buoyed by higher
prices and increased demand for oil. Generally, small-capitalization stocks outpaced
large-caps, and value stocks&#151;those with prices considered low relative to company
earnings, book value, and other measures&#151;outpaced their growth counterparts.
Inter-national stocks, particularly those in emerging markets, posted outstanding returns
compared with U.S. stocks. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Head Left-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
<P ALIGN=LEFT><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2" COLOR="Blue">YIELDS ROSE FOR SHORT-TERM BONDS, BUT FELL FOR LONG-TERM ISSUES </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Default" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=2>At the beginning of 2004, bond
investors expected higher interest rates across the maturity spectrum. The actual result,
however, was quite different at the short and long ends of the maturity range. </FONT></P>

<P ALIGN=CENTER><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=2>2</FONT></P>
<P STYLE="page-break-after:always"></P>
<!-- MARKER PAGE="sheet: 4; page: 4" -->
<HR SIZE=5 COLOR=GRAY NOSHADE>


<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=2>Yields of longer-maturity bonds closed
the year slightly below their starting points. At year-end, the 10-year U.S. Treasury note
yielded 4.22%, 3 basis points (0.03 percentage point) below its 4.25% yield at the start
of the period. Overall, the taxable investment-grade bond market, as measured by the
Lehman Brothers Aggregate Bond Index, returned 4.3%. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=2>Yields of shorter-maturity securities,
which are generally more closely tied to the Fed&#146;s interest rate moves, rose
significantly. As the Fed tightened its monetary policy to avert any significant surge in
inflation, the yield of the 3-month Treasury bill, a proxy for money market yields, rose
to 2.21%, up from 0.92% at the start of the year. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Head Left-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
<P ALIGN=LEFT><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2" COLOR="Blue">FUNDS TRACKED AN EXCELLENT
MARKET WITH PRECISION </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=2>During 2004, small-cap stocks
delivered a rousing encore to their exceptional 2003 performance. The Vanguard Small-Cap
Index Funds reflected this performance, producing returns ranging from Small-Cap
Growth&#146;s 16.1% to 23.6% for Vanguard Small-Cap Value Index Fund. Vanguard Small-Cap
Index Fund&#151;essentially, the Value and Growth Index Funds combined&#151;returned
19.9%. (All returns are for Investor Shares.) These results were superior to the average
returns produced by the funds&#146; peer groups, which consist mainly of actively managed
funds. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=2>As expected, Vanguard Quantitative
Equity Group, the funds&#146; manager, succeeded in closely tracking the returns of each
fund&#146;s target index, producing returns that were within 0.2 percentage point of the
index across all share classes. (In fact, the Institutional Shares in each fund edged past
the index return.) These results are a tribute to the portfolio construction and trading
methodologies developed and refined by Vanguard Quantitative Equity Group ever since we
launched the first index mutual fund in 1976. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=2>The tight tracking allowed investors
to make the most of a strong small-cap market. The best-performing groups in the MSCI US
Small Cap 1750 Index&#151;the benchmark for Vanguard Small-Cap Index Fund&#151;included
energy-related and raw-materials stocks, which account for a relatively small percentage
of the index&#146;s value, and large sectors such as financial services, which produced
lower, but still-impressive, returns. Weaker performers included technology stocks. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Default" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=2>The performances of both the Small-Cap
Value and Small-Cap Growth Index Funds reflected their respective weightings in these
different </FONT></P>

<P ALIGN=CENTER><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=2>3</FONT></P>
<P STYLE="page-break-after:always"></P>
<!-- MARKER PAGE="sheet: 5; page: 5" -->
<HR SIZE=5 COLOR=GRAY NOSHADE>


<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=2>industry groups. For example, the
Small-Cap Value Index Fund had a heavy weighting in financial services stocks (some 37% of
assets, on average, during the period), which returned a market-beating 24.9%. The fund
also held a relatively large weighting in the materials &amp; processing sector, which
produced high returns. Together, these sectors contributed more than 13 percentage points
to the fund&#146;s 23.6% return. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=2>The Small-Cap Growth Index Fund had
smaller commitments to these strong sectors, and a much larger weighting in the weak
technology sector. These differences accounted for much of the gap between the Growth
Index Fund&#146;s impressive 16.1% return and the Value Index Fund&#146;s remarkable 23.6%
return. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Head Left-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
<P ALIGN=LEFT><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2" COLOR="Blue">LONG-TERM RETURNS REFLECT
INDEX CHANGE </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Default" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=2>The funds&#146; longer-term results
provide some perspective on the returns offered by small-cap investing during the past
decade or, in the case of the small-cap Growth and Value Index Funds, since their 1998
inception. During the ten years ended December 31, 2004, the Small-Cap Index Fund Investor
Shares produced an annualized return of 12.3%, transforming an initial investment of
$10,000 into $31,837. Over shorter time periods&#151;in which the 2000&#150;2002 bear
market figures more prominently&#151;the Growth and Value Index Funds&#146; Investor
Shares produced annualized returns of 7.5%, and, 9.5%, respectively. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=2>The adjacent table also indicates
that the Small-Cap and Small-Cap Value Index Funds trailed the average returns of their
peer groups, while Small-Cap Growth outperformed. It would be a mistake </FONT></P>


<P ALIGN=CENTER><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=2>4</FONT></P>
<P STYLE="page-break-after:always"></P>
<!-- MARKER PAGE="sheet: 6; page: 6" -->
<HR SIZE=5 COLOR=GRAY NOSHADE>


<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=2>to make too much of these results.
Until 2003, the funds tracked indexes that were inconsistent with the way active managers
approach the small-cap market. Since May 2003, the funds have targeted indexes from MSCI
that, in our estimation, have better investment properties (lower turnover, for example)
and better represent active managers' perceptions of the small-cap market. We would
expect that, in the future, differences between the returns of the index funds and those
of active managers would depend more on costs than on varying definitions of small-cap,
growth, or value, which have been an important factor in the past. </FONT></P>


<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Head Left-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
<P ALIGN=LEFT><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2" COLOR="Blue">KEEPING OUR HEADS IN HEADY
TIMES </FONT></P>


<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=2>In each of the past four years,
small- and mid-cap stocks have dramatically outperformed large-cap stocks--although in
two of those years, small-and mid-cap returns were simply less negative than large-cap
losses. The recent environment followed a 1990s bull market for large-cap stocks, in
which investors could find no fault with the market's very largest companies. What does
this mean for your portfolio in 2005? </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=2>Simply that an investment portfolio
balanced among asset classes and diversified within each class is the only way to go. The
most devoted students of the stock market cannot reliably predict the turning of tides
that bring first one and then another market segment into favor. By maintaining a
diversified portfolio and attending to the costs you pay, you increase your ability to
ride the market's ups and downs--and ultimately to thrive--despite the unpredictable
nature of market leadership. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2" COLOR="#0000FF"><B>Beta.</B> </FONT> <FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2">A
measure of the magnitude of a fund&#146;s past share-price fluctuations in
relation to the ups and downs of a given market index. The index is assigned a
beta of 1.00. Compared with a given index, a fund with a beta of 1.20 typically
would have seen its share price rise or fall by 12% when the index rose or fell
by 10%. A fund&#146;s beta should be reviewed in conjunction with its R-squared
(see definition below). The lower the R-squared, the less correlation there is
between the fund and the index, and the less reliable beta is as an indicator
of volatility. </FONT> </P>

<HR WIDTH=100% SIZE=1 COLOR=BLACK NOSHADE>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2" COLOR="#0000FF"><B>Earnings Growth Rate.</B> </FONT> <FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2">The
average annual rate of growth in earnings over the past five years for the stocks now in a
fund. </FONT> </P>
<HR WIDTH=100% SIZE=1 COLOR=BLACK NOSHADE>
<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2" COLOR="#0000FF"><B>Expense Ratio.</B> </FONT> <FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2">The percentage
of a fund&#146;s average net assets used to pay its annual administrative and advisory
expenses. These expenses directly reduce returns to investors. </FONT> </P>
<HR WIDTH=100% SIZE=1 COLOR=BLACK NOSHADE>
<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2" COLOR="#0000FF"><B>Foreign Holdings.</B> </FONT> <FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2">The
percentage of a fund&#146;s equity assets represented by stocks or depositary receipts of
companies based outside the United States. </FONT> </P>
<HR WIDTH=100% SIZE=1 COLOR=BLACK NOSHADE>
<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2" COLOR="#0000FF"><B>Median Market Cap.</B> </FONT> <FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2">An indicator
of the size of companies in which a fund invests; the midpoint of market capitalization
(market price x shares outstanding) of a fund&#146;s stocks, weighted by the proportion of
the fund&#146;s assets invested in each stock. Stocks representing half of the fund&#146;s
assets have market capitalizations above the median, and the rest are below it. </FONT> </P>
<HR WIDTH=100% SIZE=1 COLOR=BLACK NOSHADE>
<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2" COLOR="#0000FF"><B>Price/Book Ratio.</B> </FONT> <FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2">The share
price of a stock divided by its net worth, or book value, per share. For a fund, the
weighted average price/book ratio of the stocks it holds. </FONT> </P>
<HR WIDTH=100% SIZE=1 COLOR=BLACK NOSHADE>
<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2" COLOR="#0000FF"><B>Price/Earnings Ratio.</B> </FONT> <FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2">The ratio
of a stock&#146;s current price to its per-share earnings over the past year. For a fund,
the weighted average P/E of the stocks it holds. P/E is an indicator of market
expectations about corporate prospects; the higher the P/E, the greater the expectations
for a company&#146;s future growth. </FONT> </P>
<HR WIDTH=100% SIZE=1 COLOR=BLACK NOSHADE>
<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2" COLOR="#0000FF"><B>R-Squared.</B> </FONT> <FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2">A
measure of how much of a fund&#146;s past returns can be explained by the
returns from the market in general, as measured by a given index. If a
fund&#146;s total returns were precisely synchronized with an index&#146;s
returns, its R-squared would be 1.00. If the fund&#146;s returns bore no
relationship to the index&#146;s returns, its R-squared would be 0. </FONT> </P>

<HR WIDTH=100% SIZE=1 COLOR=BLACK NOSHADE>
<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2" COLOR="#0000FF"><B>Return on Equity.</B> </FONT> <FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2">The annual
average rate of return generated by a company during the past five years for each dollar
of shareholder&#146;s equity (net income divided by shareholder&#146;s equity). For a
fund, the weighted average return on equity for the companies whose stocks it holds. </FONT> </P>
<HR WIDTH=100% SIZE=1 COLOR=BLACK NOSHADE>
<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2" COLOR="#0000FF"><B>Short-Term Reserves.</B> </FONT> <FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2">The
percentage of a fund invested in highly liquid, short-term securities that can be readily
converted to cash. </FONT> </P>
<HR WIDTH=100% SIZE=1 COLOR=BLACK NOSHADE>
<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2" COLOR="#0000FF"><B>Turnover Rate.</B> </FONT> <FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2">An indication of
the fund&#146;s trading activity. Funds with high turnover rates incur higher transaction
costs and may be more likely to distribute capital gains (which may be taxable to
investors). </FONT> </P>
<HR WIDTH=100% SIZE=1 COLOR=BLACK NOSHADE>
<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2" COLOR="#0000FF"><B>Yield.</B> </FONT> <FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2">A
snapshot of a fund&#146;s income from interest and dividends. The yield,
expressed as a percentage of the fund&#146;s net asset value, is based on
income earned over the past 30 days and is annualized, or projected forward for
the coming year. The index yield is based on the current annualized rate of
income provided by securities in the index. </FONT> </P>

<HR WIDTH=100% SIZE=1 COLOR=BLACK NOSHADE>
<P ALIGN=CENTER><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=2>11</FONT></P>
<P STYLE="page-break-after:always"></P>
<!-- MARKER PAGE="sheet: 13; page: 13" -->

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Head Left-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
<P ALIGN="Left" STYLE="background-color:aliceblue;"><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2"><BR><BR>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;<B>YOUR FUND&#146;S AFTER-TAX RETURNS</B><BR><BR> </FONT></P>

<BR>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=2>This table presents returns for your
fund both before and after taxes. The after-tax returns are shown in two ways: (1)
assuming that an investor owned the fund during the entire period and paid taxes on the
fund&#146;s distributions, and (2) assuming that an investor paid taxes on the fund&#146;s
distributions <I>and </I>sold all shares at the end of each period. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=2>Calculations are based on the highest
individual federal income tax and capital gains tax rates in effect at the times of the
distributions and the hypothetical sales. State and local taxes were not considered.
After-tax returns reflect the reduced tax rates on ordinary income (including qualified
dividend income) and short-term capital gains that became effective as of January 1, 2003,
and on long-term capital gains realized on or after May 6, 2003. (In the example, returns
after the sale of fund shares may be higher than those assuming no sale. This occurs when
the sale would have produced a capital loss. The calculation assumes that the investor
received a tax deduction for the loss.) </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=2>The table shows returns for Investor
Shares only; returns for other share classes will differ. Please note that your actual
after-tax returns will depend on your tax situation and may differ from those shown. Also
note that if you own the fund in a tax-deferred account, such as an individual retirement
account or a 401(k) plan, this information does not apply to you. Such accounts are not
subject to current taxes. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Default" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=2>Finally, keep in mind that a

results. </FONT></P>

<P ALIGN="Left" STYLE="background-color:aliceblue;"><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2"><BR><BR>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;<B>ABOUT YOUR FUND&#146;S EXPENSES</B><BR><BR> </FONT></P>

<BR>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=2>We believe it is important for you to
understand the impact of costs on your investment. All mutual funds have operating
expenses. As a shareholder of the fund, you incur ongoing costs, which include costs for
portfolio management, administrative services, and shareholder reports (like this one),
among others. Operating expenses, which are deducted from a fund&#146;s gross income,
directly reduce the investment return of the fund. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Default" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=2>A fund&#146;s expenses are expressed
as a percentage of its average net assets. This figure is known as the expense ratio. The
following examples are intended to help you understand the ongoing costs (in dollars) of
investing in your fund and to compare these costs with those of other mutual funds. The
examples are based on an investment of $1,000 made at the beginning of the period shown
and held for the entire period. </FONT></P>

<BR>

<P ALIGN=LEFT><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2" COLOR="Blue"><B>STATEMENT OF NET ASSETS&#151;INVESTMENTS SUMMARY</B></FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=2>This Statement summarizes each
fund&#146;s holdings by asset type (common stocks, bonds, etc.) and by industry sector.
Details are reported for each of the fund&#146;s 50 largest individual holdings and for
investments that, in total for any issuer, represent more than 1% of the fund&#146;s
<I>Net Assets</I>. The total value of smaller holdings is reported as a single amount
within each category. Other assets are added to, and liabilities are subtracted from, the
value of <I>Total Investments </I>to calculate the fund&#146;s <I>Net Assets</I>. Finally,
<I>Net Assets </I>are divided by the outstanding shares of the fund to arrive at its share
price, or <I>Net Asset Value (NAV) Per Share</I>. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=2>At the end of the Statement you will
find a table displaying the composition of the fund&#146;s net assets. Because all income
and any realized gains must be distributed to shareholders each year, the bulk of net
assets consists of <I>Paid-in Capital </I>(money invested by shareholders). The amounts
shown for <I>Undistributed Net Investment Income </I>and <I>Accumulated Net Realized Gains
</I>usually approximate the sums the fund had available to distribute to shareholders as
income dividends or capital gains as of the statement date, but may differ because certain
investments or transactions may be treated differently for financial statement and tax
purposes. Any <I>Accumulated Net Realized Losses</I>, and any cumulative excess of
distributions over net income or net realized gains, will appear as negative balances.
<I>Unrealized Appreciation (Depreciation) </I>is the difference between the market value
of the fund&#146;s investments and their cost, and reflects the gains (losses) that would
be realized if the fund were to sell all of its investments at their statement-date
values. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Default" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=2>Each fund provides a complete list of
its holdings four times in each fiscal year, at the quarter-ends. For the second and
fourth fiscal quarters, the complete listing of the fund&#146;s holdings is available
electronically on Vanguard.com or the Securities and Exchange Commission&#146;s website
(www.sec.gov), or you can have it mailed to you without charge by calling 1-800-662-7447.
For the first and third fiscal quarters, the fund files the lists with the SEC on Form
N-Q. Shareholders can look up the fund&#146;s Forms N-Q on the SEC&#146;s website; Forms
N-Q may also be reviewed and copied at the SEC&#146;s Public Reference Room (see the back
cover of this report for further information). </FONT></P>

<H1 ALIGN=LEFT><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2" COLOR="Blue">NOTES TO FINANCIAL STATEMENTS </FONT></H1>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=2>Vanguard Small-Cap Index, Small-Cap Growth
Index, and Small-Cap Value Index Funds are registered under the Investment Company Act of
1940 as open-end investment companies, or mutual funds. The Small-Cap Index Fund offers
four classes of shares: Investor Shares, Admiral Shares, Institutional Shares, and VIPER
Shares. The Small-Cap Growth Index and Small-Cap Value Index Funds each offer three
classes of shares, Investor Shares, Institutional Shares, and VIPER Shares. Investor
Shares are available to any investor who meets the fund&#146;s minimum purchase
requirements. Admiral Shares are designed for investors who meet certain administrative,
servicing, tenure, and account-size criteria. Institutional Shares are designed for
investors who meet certain administrative and servicing criteria and invest a minimum of
$10 million. VIPER Shares are listed for trading on the American Stock Exchange; they can
be purchased and sold through a broker. The Small-Cap Index, Small-Cap Growth Index, and
Small-Cap Value Index Funds VIPER Shares were first issued on January 26, 2004, and
offered to the public on January 30, 2004. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2" COLOR="#0000FF"><B>A.</B> </FONT> <FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2">The following
significant accounting policies conform to generally accepted accounting
principles for U.S. mutual funds. The funds consistently follow such policies
in preparing their financial statements. </FONT> </P>



          <BR>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para (List) Hang Lvl 3-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
     <TABLE WIDTH=100% CELLPADDING=0 CELLSPACING=0 BORDER=0>
          <TR VALIGN=TOP>
          <TD WIDTH=3%><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=2><B>1.</B> </FONT></TD>
          <TD WIDTH=97%><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=2>
          <B>Security Valuation: </B>Securities are valued as of the close of trading on
          the New York Stock Exchange (generally 4:00 p.m., Eastern time) on the valuation
          date. Equity securities are valued at the latest quoted sales prices or official
          closing prices taken from the primary market in which each security trades; such
          securities not traded on the valuation date are valued at the mean of the latest
          quoted bid and asked prices. Securities for which market quotations are not
          readily available, or whose values have been materially affected by events
          occurring before the fund&#146;s pricing time but after the close of the
          securities&#146; primary markets, are valued by methods deemed by the board of
          trustees to represent fair value. Investments in Vanguard&reg; Market Liquidity
          Fund are valued at that fund&#146;s net asset value. Temporary cash investments
          acquired over 60 days to maturity are valued using the latest bid prices or
          using valuations based on a matrix system (which considers such factors as
          security prices, yields, maturities, and ratings), both as furnished by
          independent pricing services. Other temporary cash investments are valued at
          amortized cost, which approximates market value. </FONT></TD>
          </TR>
          </TABLE>
          <BR>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para (List) Hang Lvl 3-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
     <TABLE WIDTH=100% CELLPADDING=0 CELLSPACING=0 BORDER=0>
          <TR VALIGN=TOP>
          <TD WIDTH=3%><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=2><B>2.</B> </FONT></TD>
          <TD WIDTH=97%><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=2>
          <B>Futures Contracts: </B>The funds use Russell 2000 Index futures contracts to
          a limited extent, with the objectives of maintaining full exposure to the stock
          market, enhancing returns, maintaining liquidity, and minimizing transaction
          costs. A fund may purchase futures contracts to immediately invest incoming cash
          in the market, or sell futures in response to cash outflows, thereby simulating
          a fully invested position in the underlying index while maintaining a cash
          balance for liquidity. A fund may seek to enhance returns by using futures
          contracts instead of the underlying securities when futures are believed to be
          priced more attractively than the underlying securities. The primary risks
          associated with the use of futures contracts are imperfect correlation between
          changes in market values of stocks held by the fund and the prices of futures
          contracts, and the possibility of an illiquid market. </FONT></TD>
          </TR>
          </TABLE>
          <BR>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 4-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
<TABLE WIDTH=100% CELLPADDING=0 CELLSPACING=0 BORDER=0>
<TR VALIGN=TOP>
<TD WIDTH=3%>&nbsp;</TD>
<TD WIDTH=97%><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=2>
Futures
contracts are valued at their quoted daily settlement prices. The aggregate principal
amounts of the contracts are not recorded in the financial statements. Fluctuations in the
value of the contracts are recorded in the Statement of Net Assets as an asset (liability)
and in the Statement of Operations as unrealized appreciation (depreciation) until the
contracts are closed, when they are recorded as realized futures gains (losses).</FONT></TD>
</TR>
</TABLE>
<BR>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para (List) Hang Lvl 3-Arial" FSL="Default" -->

          <TD WIDTH=97%><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=2>
          <B>Repurchase Agreements: </B>Each fund, along with other members of The
          Vanguard Group, may transfer uninvested cash balances into a pooled cash
          account, which is invested in repurchase agreements secured by U.S. government
          securities. Securities pledged as collateral for repurchase agreements are held
          by a custodian bank until the agreements mature. Each agreement requires that
          the market value of the collateral be sufficient to cover payments of interest
          and principal; </FONT></TD>
          </TR>
          </TABLE>

          <B>Other: </B>Dividend income is recorded on the ex-dividend date. Interest

          securities are bought or sold. Costs used to determine realized gains (losses)

          each class separately bears certain class-specific expenses related to
          maintenance of shareholder accounts (included in Management and Administrative

          allocated to each class of shares based on a method approved by the board of

<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2" COLOR="#0000FF"><B>C.</B> </FONT><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2">Distributions
are determined on a tax basis and may differ from net investment income and
realized capital gains for financial reporting purposes. Differences may be
permanent or temporary. Permanent differences are reclassified among capital
accounts in the financial statements to reflect their tax character. Temporary
differences arise when certain items of income, expense, gain, or loss are
recognized in different periods for financial statement and tax purposes; these
differences will reverse at some time in the future. Differences in
classification may also result from the treatment of short-term gains as
ordinary income for tax purposes. </FONT> </P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Default" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="3" COLOR="#0000FF">The U.S. stock market started and
ended 2004 with a strong surge and retreated in between. The result was a 12.6% gain for
the broad market, as measured by the Dow Jones Wilshire 5000 Composite Index. Mid- and
small-capitalization stocks enjoyed significantly higher returns. The Investor Shares of
Vanguard Extended Market Index Fund and Vanguard Mid-Cap Index Fund gained 18.7% and
20.4%, respectively. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Default" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=2>As the adjacent table shows, both
funds fulfilled their objectives of closely tracking their target indexes. Both funds also
significantly outperformed the average mid-cap core mutual fund. Most funds in this
category are actively managed and carry higher expenses than either of the Vanguard
mid-cap portfolios. The VIPER Shares within the Mid-Cap Index Fund were launched on
January 26, 2004, missing the year&#146;s strong early weeks for stock returns. The new
shares met their objective of capturing the index&#146;s performance during the period
under review. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=2>The U.S. stock market rallied
following the presidential election in November to post a second consecutive year of solid
returns. The gains in the final two months of 2004 capped a year that began with solid
advances in stock indexes but was marked in the middle months by investors&#146;
uncertainty about the sustainability of economic growth. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=2>Gains came in many sectors of the
market. The strongest performers were energy-related stocks, which were buoyed by higher
prices and increased demand for oil. Generally, small-cap stocks outpaced large-caps, and
value stocks&#151;those with prices considered low relative to company earnings, book
value, and other measures&#151;outpaced their growth counterparts. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=2>International stocks, particularly
those in emerging markets, posted outstanding returns compared with U.S. stocks. The
strong gains abroad were enhanced for investors in the United States by the weakening of
the U.S. dollar against most other major currencies. (A weaker dollar means that returns
in other currencies translate into more dollars for U.S.-based investors.) </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Head Left-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
<P ALIGN=LEFT><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2" COLOR="#0000FF"><B>YIELDS ROSE FOR SHORT-TERM
BONDS, FELL FOR LONG-TERM ISSUES</B> </FONT> </P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Default" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=2>At the beginning of 2004, bond
investors expected the year to bring higher interest rates across the maturity spectrum.
Their expectations were based on increasingly strong economic reports, rising corporate
profits, and a belief that the Federal Reserve Board would soon raise the target for
short-term interest rates to keep inflation at bay. The actual result, however, was quite
different at the short and long ends of the maturity range. </FONT></P>


<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Page Number Center" FSL="Project" -->
<P ALIGN="Left"><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=1> 2</FONT></P>
<P STYLE="page-break-after:always">
</P>

<!-- MARKER PAGE="sheet: 4; page: 4" -->
<HR SIZE=5 COLOR=GRAY NOSHADE>



<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=2>Yields of longer-maturity bonds closed
the year slightly below their starting points. A series of disappointments in the labor
market, record prices for crude oil, and continuing geopolitical turmoil kept bond market
volatility high. At the year-end, the 10-year U.S. Treasury note yielded 4.22%, 3 basis
points (0.03 percentage point) below its 4.25% yield at the start of the period. Overall,
the taxable investment-grade bond market, as measured by the Lehman Brothers Aggregate
Bond Index, returned 4.3%. Across the maturity spectrum, corporate bonds, particularly
those from below-investment-grade issuers, generally did better than government
securities. The Lehman High Yield Index returned 11.1%. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Default" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=2>Yields of shorter-maturity securities,
which are generally more closely tied to the Fed&#146;s interest rate moves, rose
significantly. As anticipated, the Fed began to tighten monetary policy to prevent any
significant surge in inflation. Beginning in June, the Fed raised its target for the
federal funds rate from 1.00%, a historical low, to 2.25% through five separate
quarter-point increases. The yield of the 3-month Treasury bill, a proxy for money market
yields, more than doubled during the 12 months, from 0.92% to 2.21%. </FONT></P>

<P ALIGN=LEFT><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2" COLOR="#0000FF"><B>REBOUND ENJOYED ACROSS
MOST INDUSTRY GROUPINGS</B> </FONT> </P>

<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=2>The year-end rally spanned industry
sectors, with the highest returns coming from sectors tied to the production of energy and
commodities. These sectors, however, are not large weightings in the Vanguard mid-cap
index funds. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Default" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=2>For both the Extended Market and
Mid-Cap Index Funds, financial services and consumer discretionary stocks make up the
largest portions of the portfolios (approximately 50% at the year-end for </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Page Number Center" FSL="Project" -->
<P ALIGN="Right"><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=1>3 </FONT></P>

<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=2>Extended Market and 40% for Mid-Cap).
The strong performance of these two sectors accounted for half of the Extended Market
Index Fund&#146;s gain and just under half of the Mid-Cap Index Fund&#146;s return. Among
top performers within financial services were companies that own and operate commercial
and residential real estate. Consumer discretionary stocks (including retailers,
restaurants, and entertainment purveyors) typically do well when the economy picks up
steam as pent-up demand for goods and services is released; these stocks thrived in
2004&#145;s improving climate. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=2>The volatile technology sector served
as a drag on both funds, although the sector&#146;s underperformance was much more
pronounced among smaller stocks. Tech stocks produced a negative return in the Extended
Market Index Fund, reflecting the small-cap stocks represented in the Dow Jones Wilshire
4500 Index. This was the lone negative sector performance in either fund. Declines by
bellwether tech stocks Intel and Cisco Systems caused a ripple effect, knocking down
returns for the many smaller suppliers and niche competitors in the semiconductor and
router businesses. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Head Left-Arial" FSL="Project" -->

by marginally outpacing their benchmarks over longer periods. This is a significant feat,
given that indexes bear none of the operating or transaction costs that detract from a
mutual fund&#146;s return. The Vanguard funds&#146; achievement reflects two competitive
advantages: </FONT></P>

<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=2>The Mid-Cap Index Fund&#146;s superior
return can be partly explained by its lower expense ratio and its shorter life span, in
which the bear market features prominently. By adhering to its benchmark, the fund avoided
exposure to untested companies not in the index&#151;companies that many active managers
took a chance on, to their disadvantage. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Head Left-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
<P ALIGN=LEFT><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE="2" COLOR="#0000FF"><B>KEEPING OUR HEADS IN HEADY
TIMES</B> </FONT> </P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=2>In each of the past four years, small-
and mid-cap stocks have dramatically outperformed large-cap stocks&#151;although in two of
those years, returns were simply less negative for small- and mid-cap stocks than for
bigger companies. The recent environment followed a 1990s bull market for large-cap
stocks, in which investors could find no fault with the market&#146;s largest companies.
What does this mean for your portfolio in 2005? </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Default" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=2>Simply that a well-considered
strategy, balanced among asset classes and diversified within each class, is the only way
to go. The most devoted students of the stock market cannot reliably predict the turning
of tides that bring first one and then another market segment </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Page Number Center" FSL="Project" -->
<P ALIGN="Right"><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=1>5 </FONT></P>
<P STYLE="page-break-after:always">
</P>

<!-- MARKER PAGE="sheet: 7; page: 7" -->
<HR SIZE=5 COLOR=GRAY NOSHADE>



<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
<P><FONT FACE="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" SIZE=2>into favor. By maintaining a
diversified portfolio and attending to the costs you pay, you increase your ability to
ride the market&#146;s ups and downs&#151;and ultimately to thrive&#151;despite the
unpredictable nature of market leadership. </FONT></P>
